prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which neutral atoms trapped at the magic wavelength reach fractional uncertainties near 1e-18

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B030 alone, credited to Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye. After reading the full first round, the case rests on one sentence that I propose the committee record in answer to the chair's first question. The 2005 prize honoured the frequency comb as a ruler and the 2012 prize honoured quantum control of individual trapped ions, whereas the lattice clock is a different physical scheme: a magic-wavelength optical lattice whose trapping light shift cancels for the clock transition, so that many neutral atoms can be interrogated together at the accuracy previously associated only with single ions. That idea, and its realization through the systematic evaluation that brought several laboratories to fractional uncertainties near 1e-18, is what the citation should name. It is not a statement about optical clocks or timekeeping in general. The case does not depend on the redefinition of the second; it rests on demonstrated performance and on independent agreement between clocks in several countries. The discovery content that Danielsson asked for is real and already used: tests of gravitational redshift over millimetre-to-centimetre height differences, searches for varying constants and for ultralight dark matter, and the many-body clock physics Ye's group opened. On citation scope, I support the wording that names the magic-wavelength lattice, with the 1e-18 level as the demonstration, over the bare invention-and-realization wording. This is a judgement within the atomic-physics community that I know, not a fact I can verify from the supplied text beyond what the profiles and nominations state.
statement.case_against: The strongest remaining reservations are the ones the chair listed, and I do not think any of them is resolved by agreement alone. First, overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes is a matter of judgement: Mehlig is right that the methods (laser spectroscopy, cooling and trapping) are close, so the citation must carry the distinction explicitly. Second, the pair omits real contributors. Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow and the ion-clock groups advanced accuracy and comparison, and I cannot show from the supplied text that Katori's proposal and Ye's realization outweigh them; the two-name allocation is a defensible cut, not a clean fact, as Pearce asked it be described. Third, part of the 1e-18 record is refinement of an existing concept, so the prize must honour the invention and its realization and not a sequence of performance records. Finally, the redefinition of the second has not happened, so the practical culmination is still prospective, although I do not regard that as a reason to delay.

responses.point: Danielsson moved B030 up from sixth after round 1 but asks that the citation state what the clocks have enabled, otherwise the metrology-overlap objection stays open, and he doubts the three-name cut for B004 that drops Greiner.
responses.response: I agree that the citation should not leave the discovery content implicit, and I would let the invention-and-realization wording carry it by naming the magic-wavelength lattice and the 1e-18 level, with the fundamental-physics tests recorded in the committee's motivation rather than the citation text. On B004 you are right and I now concede the point: I would not defend Bloch, Zoller and Esslinger against Bloch, Greiner and Zoller, and my own round-1 list conceded as much. That is a change in how I would fill B004 as an alternative, not a change in my preferred prize.

responses.point: Mehlig says the 2005 and 2012 citations are close enough in method (spectroscopy, laser cooling and trapping) that overlap should not be treated as closed, and asks that the citation emphasise neutral atoms at the magic wavelength in large ensembles.
responses.response: I take that seriously and I think it is the right way to treat the overlap objection: not as settled by assertion, but answered in the wording. My answer to the chair is that the lattice clock is not a refinement of the comb or of ion control, because the new element is the engineered cancellation of the trap light shift at the magic wavelength together with ensemble statistics. If the committee judges that this sentence does not distinguish the work from the earlier prizes, then the overlap would count against B030 and I would want to revisit B004 or B058. I do not reach that conclusion, but I accept it as a legitimate test rather than a formality.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, asks that the Katori and Ye allocation be called a judgement rather than a clean fact, presses on Lemonde, Ludlow and the other omitted contributors, and prefers IceCube (B020) as his first alternative.
responses.response: I accept the wording and have used it above: the pair is a defensible allocation, not an established fact, and I will not describe it as clean to the point of excluding Lemonde, Lisdat or Ludlow. On the question of evidence, I would need to see the proposal and first demonstrations dated against the early independent lattice-clock work, and an assessment of how far the accuracy records depended on each group, before I would change the pair; nothing in the round-1 files supplies that. On B020 I still hold that it is a genuine new observational window, but credit among Halzen, Karle and Spiering, and the AMANDA lineage, is less settled than for B030, so I keep it outside my alternatives while remaining willing to hear a clearer attribution rule.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers Car-Parrinello (B022) alone but names B030 as his first alternative, would defer to Lindroth and me on technical priority, and says the redefinition of the second will not change the science.
responses.response: Thank you for separating merit from field proximity; I agree the redefinition is a decision that follows the physics, so the case should be recorded as resting on demonstrated performance alone. On B022 my position is unchanged in substance: the two-name attribution is excellent and the maturity is beyond doubt, but whether a computational method is a physics invention remains for the committee to decide, and I am not the right person to settle it. If you stay on B022 as a competing configuration, please say so explicitly in the vote, so that the discussion records whether your support for B030 is a first choice or only a fallback.

responses.point: Lindroth would not name Lemonde in the citation and would not lean on the redefinition of the second, resting the prize on the magic-wavelength concept and its realization.
responses.response: I agree on both points and my citation follows them. Where I would qualify your position slightly is that omitting Lemonde from the citation is not the same as saying his contribution was minor; the committee's motivation should be careful on this so we do not assert more precision about priority than the text supports. I also share your view that the discovery-versus-application objection is answered by the new physics of light shifts, forbidden transitions and many-body effects.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept the one-sentence distinction from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, or whether Mehlig, Danielsson and Pearce judge the overlap still disqualifying.

The correct boundary between the credited pair and Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow and the ion-clock groups; I cannot settle it from the supplied text and would need the early chronology of lattice-clock proposals and demonstrations.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second should delay recognition; I think not, but I accept that others may weigh it differently.

If B030 were set aside, my single alternative would be B004, with Bloch, Greiner and Zoller as the more defensible trio, though the credit problem (including Esslinger and Jaksch) remains unresolved, followed by B058.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure: I trained in Lund laser spectroscopy and spent a research stay in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, the scientific lineage from which Jun Ye's group at JILA developed. This is a documented professional connection relevant to B030; the profile shows no direct collaboration, supervisory or institutional tie to Katori or Ye, and nothing in round 1 changes that. I also work in atomic physics and quantum optics, so B004 (including Zoller) lies in a neighbouring community with European quantum-memory and quantum-information collaborations, though I know of no specific documented relationship to Bloch, Greiner or Zoller. I do not consider recusal necessary and will leave that to the chair, who may wish to record the Boulder lineage.
